source_title: Creative project reimagines history from First Nations perspective
source_excerpt:
Address to the Nations co-creators David Pledger and Tony Briggs with actor Sherry-Lee Watson. ( Supplied: Declan Bailey )
In the alternate timeline imagined by Address to the Nations, colonisation didn't happen in Australia, and the country is guided by a Ministry of Elders who oversee a democratic system of government.
The project is the brainchild of Yorta Yorta/Wurundjeri actor, writer, producer and director Tony Briggs, best known for creating and writing the musical comedy film, The Sapphires, and his close friend, award-winning artist, curator, producer and writer David Pledger.
To tell the story, which stretches over 300 years, Briggs and Pledger have begun building a portfolio with an art series, TV show, theatre production and video game part of the offering.
Actor Kelton Pell plays the 1940 First Minister Ngapa Marratha in Address to the Nations. ( Supplied: Declan Bailey )
They've established the collaborative practice Tomorrow's Pasts under the moniker briggsnpledger and have built a universe that borrows from genres such as alternate futurism, counter-factual storytelling and science fiction to create an alternate Australian history as a way to imagine a better future.
"What if you could travel back in time? What would you do? We had many conversations over a long period of time around that very question," Briggs told PM .
"One of the things that kept popping up was, well, we think we'd like to sort of warn people of the mistakes.
"We can prompt you, [but] you have to find these mistakes for yourself and collect information and come forward and hopefully you come forward with the correct answers for humanity, if you like, [for] all of us, not just a certain sector of the community."
As part of the story, in 2063, the Ministry of Elders, which governs the Great Southern Nations (Australia in our current timeline) sends a message stick 300 years into the past to warn First Nations peoples about the arrival of outsiders (called The Accelerationists) and the potential for race-based conflicts.
The information sent into the past allows for the development of technology, giving First Nations peoples the power to keep control over their lands, regardless of the ambitions of outsiders.
Sherry-Lee Watson plays the 2022 First Minister Alinta Maris in Address to the Nations. ( Supplied: Declan Bailey )
The title of the project invokes the addresses the First Ministers (prime ministers in our timeline) deliver to the country.
Three out of the 10 addresses have so far been recorded. These are set in 1940, 1981 and 2022.
"1940 sets up what's about to happen, which is a race-based civil war in which Aboriginal Australia and its allies [are] contested by a group of [domestic] techno-fascists called the Accelerationists," Pledger told PM.
"Our First Minister in 1981 announces the beginning of the race-based civil war and over the subsequent 40 years there is a contest between Aboriginal Australians [and] allies, and the Accelerationists for sovereignty of the country."
Pledger says technology has a different trajectory in the alternate timeline.
"You have various changes in leadership, and the most significant one is the one that leads us up to the 2022 Address to the Nations, in which a young woman, Alinta Maris, who's a kind of tech genius, who has created HapTik Media and Blockchain over the preceding 20 years, in 2022, she develops non-lethal warfare, which brings the war to an end."
The visual art series was launched in June and has been shown at special screenings in Canberra and Melbourne and will next year be programmed into Australia's premier Indigenous-led film festival, the Birrarangga Film Festival.
Founder and CEO of Indigital Mikaela Jade described the work as "incredible".
"We all have the agency and autonomy to be able to help create this future and I think this is a great catalyst for conversations," she said.
Author and historian Margo Ngawa Neale picked up on the close friendship between Briggs and Pledger.
"And these two fellas, their relationship is in fact in itself a model for what Address to the Nations can be."
Impossible choice between friendship and community
Briggs and Pledger first worked together about 25 years ago on the multimedia theatre production K , which Pledger wrote and directed and Briggs starred in.
Tony Briggs and David Pledger have known each other for about 25 years. ( Supplied: Declan Bailey )
They became fast friends, and their bond sparked the initial idea for Address to the Nations.
"When David and I first started talking about this idea, it was at the height of the Black Lives Matter movement and a question popped up around having to make a choice," Briggs said.
"What if either of us had to make a choice between our friendships based on our race, based on the colour of our skin, if we were forced to do it?
"And both of us, we both said, well, the first priority will be our families, number one.
"So, we talked around all of that and we sort of imagined the worst being forced upon us and it just sort of kind of cracked open this interesting conversation."
Ultimately, the two agreed they would fight to maintain their close friendship because, as Pledger says, they are like family.
"Family's not just about blood," Pledger said.
David Pledger says family can also be defined as a close friend you're not biologically related to. ( Supplied: Declan Bailey )
"Family's about an extension of the sorts of relationships that you can call familial at least.
"So, it gets very sticky with that kind of question because where's the friendship stop and the family begin?
"And I think that's one of the things where we found so interesting in these sort of discussions is the threshold keeps moving and hopefully it dissolves."
